name: amp

members.name: custom_bwd
members.signature: custom_bwd(bwd: Callable[..., R] | None = None, device_type: str)
members.summary: Decorate a custom `Function.backward` to run in its `forward`'s autocast state.
members.extended:
The decorated `backward` runs inside an autocast scope matching the one
`custom_fwd` recorded — on at the same dtype, or off — whatever
scope `.backward()` was called from, so the arithmetic on the gradient
and the tensors `forward` saved sees the dtypes it saw going forward.

parameters.name: bwd
parameters.description: The `backward` to decorate; leave it out to get the decorator.

parameters.name: device_type
parameters.description:
`"metal"` or `"cpu"`, the same as `forward`'s.  Keyword-only
and required.

returns.description: The decorated `backward` (`bwd` given), or the decorator.

raises.description:
When the decorated `backward` runs: if `forward` was not
decorated with `custom_fwd`, or was with another
`device_type`.

see_also.name: custom_fwd
see_also.description: the matching `forward` decorator, with a worked example.

members.name: custom_fwd
members.signature: custom_fwd(fwd: Callable[..., R] | None = None, device_type: str, cast_inputs: dtype | None = None)
members.summary: Decorate a custom `Function.forward` so `backward` can follow its autocast state.
members.extended:
Under `lucid.amp.autocast` an op inside `forward` computes in
half precision, so its result and the gradient that comes back are half
precision while the tensors `forward` saved are still float32 — and the
`backward`'s arithmetic on the pair fails.  The decorated `forward`
stores the autocast state of `device_type` on `ctx`; decorate
`backward` with `custom_bwd` to run it in that state.

Used bare as `custom_fwd(fwd, device_type=...)` or, as a decorator
factory, `@custom_fwd(device_type=...)` placed under `@staticmethod`.

parameters.name: fwd
parameters.description: The `forward` to decorate; leave it out to get the decorator.

parameters.name: device_type
parameters.description:
`"metal"` or `"cpu"`; anything else raises `ValueError`.
Keyword-only and required.

parameters.name: cast_inputs
parameters.description:
When given and autocast is enabled on `device_type` at the call,
every floating-point tensor argument on that device (float64
excepted) is cast to this dtype — nested lists, tuples and dicts
included — and `forward` runs with autocast **off**; `backward`
then runs with it off too.  `None` (default) leaves the inputs
alone and runs `forward` in the caller's state.  Outside an
autocast scope `cast_inputs` does nothing.

returns.description: The decorated `forward` (`fwd` given), or the decorator.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.amp import autocast, custom_bwd, custom_fwd
>>> from lucid.autograd import Function
>>> class MatMul(Function):
...     @staticmethod
...     @custom_fwd(device_type="cpu")
...     def forward(ctx, a, b):
...         ctx.save_for_backward(a, b)
...         return a @ b
...     @staticmethod
...     @custom_bwd(device_type="cpu")
...     def backward(ctx, grad):
...         a, b = ctx.saved_tensors
...         return grad @ b.mT, a.mT @ grad
>>> a = lucid.randn(3, 4, requires_grad=True)
>>> b = lucid.randn(4, 2, requires_grad=True)
>>> with autocast("cpu", dtype=lucid.bfloat16):
...     y = MatMul.apply(a, b)
>>> y.dtype
lucid.bfloat16
>>> y.float().sum().backward()
>>> a.grad.dtype
lucid.float32

see_also.name: lucid.amp.autocast
see_also.description: the scope whose state is recorded.

methods.name: __enter__
methods.summary: Activate (or disable) the autocast scope and return `self`.
methods.extended:
Constructing the engine `AutocastGuard` sets the AMP state for
`self._device_type` to `(enabled, dtype)` and records the state
it replaced; the guard is kept until `__exit__`.

methods.name: __exit__
methods.summary: Restore the AMP state that was active when the scope was entered.
methods.extended:
Releases the guard `__enter__` made.  Its destructor runs at
once and puts back the state it recorded, so the scope ends here
rather than whenever the `autocast` object is collected.
Exceptions propagate.

methods.name: __call__
methods.summary: Use as a function decorator.
methods.extended:
Every call of the decorated function runs inside this scope — the
same `device_type`, `dtype` and `enabled` — and leaves it on
return or on an exception.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: The function to wrap.

returns.description: `fn` wrapped so that each call enters and exits the scope.

methods.name: get_autocast_dtype
methods.summary: Return the currently active autocast dtype (for `device_type` if given), or None.

members.summary: Enable automatic mixed-precision computation inside a context.
members.extended:
Operations that opt into AMP (matmul, conv, attention, …) cast their
inputs to the target lower-precision dtype on entry, reducing memory
pressure and — on Metal — improving throughput by activating the
M-series GPU's half-precision tensor pipelines.  Cast points are
inserted *only* at op boundaries; activations themselves are stored
in the lower-precision dtype but accumulator and reduction state stay
in float32 to preserve numerical fidelity (the standard "mixed" recipe).

Leaving the scope restores exactly the state it was entered from —
autocast off, or the enclosing scope's dtype — whether it is left
normally or by an exception, and however long the `autocast` object
itself lives on afterwards.  One object can be entered again after it
exits, entered while it is already active (each entry is undone by its
own exit), and used as a decorator.  `enabled=False` disables
autocast on `device_type` for the duration of the scope while leaving
the other device's autocast state untouched.

Autocast state is tracked independently per device (`"metal"` vs
`"cpu"`) on each thread.

parameters.name: device_type
parameters.description:
Device the autocast scope applies to.  `"metal"` (GPU stream,
default) or `"cpu"` (Accelerate stream); anything else raises
`ValueError`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description:
Lower-precision dtype that supported ops cast inputs to inside
the scope.  Default `lucid.float16` on `"metal"` and
`lucid.bfloat16` on `"cpu"` (matching the reference
framework).

parameters.name: enabled
parameters.description:
When `False` autocast is disabled on `device_type` inside the
scope — useful for ablation or forcing full precision in a nested
subregion.  Default `True`.

examples:
Context-manager form (typical training loop):
>>> import lucid
>>> import lucid.nn as nn
>>> model = nn.Linear(4, 2).to("metal")
>>> x = lucid.randn(8, 4, device="metal")
>>> with lucid.amp.autocast():
...     output = model(x)            # ops cast to float16 inside
>>> output.dtype
lucid.float16
Decorator form (every call wraps itself in a fresh scope):
>>> @lucid.amp.autocast()
... def predict(x):
...     return model(x)
>>> predict(x).dtype
lucid.float16
Nested scopes restore the outer dtype on exit:
>>> a = lucid.randn(2, 2, device="metal")
>>> with lucid.amp.autocast(dtype=lucid.float16):
...     print((a @ a).dtype)  # fp16 here
...     with lucid.amp.autocast(dtype=lucid.bfloat16):
...         print((a @ a).dtype)  # bf16 here
...     print((a @ a).dtype)  # back to fp16 — prior guard reinstalled
lucid.float16
lucid.bfloat16
lucid.float16
notes:
`dtype` must be one the device can autocast to: `lucid.float16`
or `lucid.bfloat16` on both `"metal"` and `"cpu"`.  Any other
dtype — an integer, `bool`, `float32`, `float64` — emits a
`UserWarning` when the scope is created and turns it into one with
`enabled=False`, as the reference framework does, so the ops inside run
in the dtype of their inputs rather than silently in the unsupported one.
The decorator form and nested scopes inherit this: they are built through
the same constructor.  A scope that was `enabled=False` already does not
warn.

members.name: is_autocast_available
members.summary: Whether an autocast scope can be opened on `device_type`.

parameters.name: device_type
parameters.description: A device type name.

returns.description:
`True` for `"metal"` and `"cpu"`, the two devices
`autocast` accepts; `False` for any other name (it is a
query, so an unknown name is an answer rather than an error).

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> lucid.amp.is_autocast_available("cpu")
True
>>> lucid.amp.is_autocast_available("tpu")
False

methods.name: scale
methods.summary: Multiply outputs by the current scale factor.

parameters.name: outputs
parameters.description: A Tensor or list of Tensors to scale.

returns.description: Scaled Tensor(s) — same structure as input.

methods.name: unscale_
methods.summary: Divide the optimizer's gradients by the current scale, in place.
methods.extended:
Call it between `backward()` and `step` when the real
gradients are needed — to clip them, or to inspect their norm.  The
scaler records that this optimizer's gradients are unscaled, so the
`step` that follows does not divide them again.

parameters.name: optimizer
parameters.description: The optimizer whose parameters' gradients are unscaled.

raises.description:
If `unscale_` already ran for `optimizer` since the last
`update`, or `step` already ran for it.

If any of `optimizer`'s gradients is float16.  Nothing is
unscaled and the optimizer's stage does not change.

If any of `optimizer`'s gradients is complex, again before
anything is unscaled.

notes:
Every gradient is divided, including those of a parameter whose
gradient holds an `inf` / `NaN` (those entries stay non-finite);
the overflow is recorded for this optimizer and its `step`
is skipped.

Every gradient keeps its dtype.  A bfloat16 gradient is cast to
float32, divided and finiteness-checked there, then rounded back to
bfloat16 once.  float32 and float64 gradients are unscaled in their
own dtype.

Float16 gradients are refused, as the reference framework refuses
them.  They come from float16 *parameters*, and loss scaling
assumes float32 master weights: `lucid.amp.autocast` runs
the forward in half precision while the parameters and their
gradients stay float32.  Dividing a float16 gradient by the default
scale `2**16` puts most of its entries below float16's smallest
normal value `6.1e-5`.  Metal flushes those subnormals to zero.
Keep the parameters in float32 and let `lucid.amp.autocast`
choose the half-precision ops.

methods.name: step
methods.signature: step(optimizer: Optimizer, args: object = (), kwargs: object = {})
methods.summary: Unscale the gradients if needed, then step unless they overflowed.
methods.extended:
If `unscale_` already ran for `optimizer` in this iteration
its gradients are used as they are; otherwise they are unscaled
here.  The optimizer's `step()` is skipped when its gradients held
an `inf` or `NaN`.

parameters.name: optimizer
parameters.description: The optimizer to step.

parameters.name: *args
parameters.description: Forwarded to `optimizer.step()`.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.description:
Forwarded to `optimizer.step()`.  `closure` is rejected
while the scaler is enabled: a closure re-runs `backward()`
and its gradients would never be unscaled.

returns.description:
What `optimizer.step()` returned, or `None` when the step
was skipped.

raises.description:
If `step` already ran for `optimizer` since the last
`update`, or `closure` is passed while enabled.

If the gradients still need unscaling and one of them is
float16 — see `unscale_`.

If the gradients still need unscaling and one of them is
complex.

methods.name: update
methods.summary: Update the scale factor and start the next iteration.
methods.extended:
If a scale is provided, it is set directly. Otherwise, the scale
is reduced by `backoff_factor` if any optimizer's gradients
overflowed since the last update, or grown by `growth_factor`
after `growth_interval` overflow-free updates.  Either way every
optimizer returns to the state where `unscale_` and
`step` may be called again.

members.summary: Dynamic loss-scaling helper for mixed-precision training.
members.extended:
Mixed-precision training runs the forward pass in fp16 to halve
memory bandwidth and exploit fp16-fast hardware paths, but
fp16's narrow dynamic range causes small gradients to underflow to
zero — the network stops learning.  `GradScaler` works
around this by multiplying the loss by a large constant $s$
before backpropagation:

$$
\tilde{L} = s \cdot L, \qquad
\frac{\partial \tilde{L}}{\partial \theta}
= s \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}.
$$

The scaled gradients sit comfortably inside fp16's representable
range; before the optimizer step they are unscaled by $1/s$
in fp32 so the update is mathematically equivalent to ordinary
training.

The scale itself is adapted dynamically.  After every step the
unscaled gradients are checked for `inf` / `NaN`:

* **Overflow detected** — the step is skipped and $s$ is
  multiplied by `backoff_factor` (typically `0.5`).
* **No overflow for `growth_interval` consecutive steps** —
  $s$ is multiplied by `growth_factor` (typically `2.0`).

This produces a sawtooth schedule that tracks the largest scale
the current gradient distribution can tolerate.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description:
The device the scaler is for, `'metal'` or `'cpu'`; anything
else raises `ValueError`.  The first parameter, as in the
reference framework.  Checked at construction only — each gradient
is unscaled on the device it lives on.

parameters.name: init_scale
parameters.description: Initial loss scaling factor applied by `scale`.

parameters.name: growth_factor
parameters.description:
Multiplier applied to the scale after `growth_interval`
consecutive non-overflowing steps.  Must be `> 1.0`.

parameters.name: backoff_factor
parameters.description:
Multiplier applied when an `inf` / `NaN` gradient is
detected.  Must be in `(0, 1)`.

parameters.name: growth_interval
parameters.description: Number of overflow-free steps required before the scale grows.

parameters.name: enabled
parameters.description:
When `False` the scaler degenerates into a transparent
pass-through — `scale` returns its input unchanged,
`step` calls the optimizer directly, `update` is a
no-op, `get_scale` is `1.0` and `state_dict` is
empty.

raises.description:
If `device` is neither `'metal'` nor `'cpu'`, or, for an
enabled scaler, `growth_factor <= 1.0` or `backoff_factor >= 1.0`.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> import lucid.nn as nn
>>> import lucid.optim as optim
>>> from lucid.amp import GradScaler, autocast
>>> model = nn.Linear(4, 1).to("metal")
>>> optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
>>> loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
>>> dataloader = [
...     (lucid.randn(8, 4, device="metal"), lucid.randn(8, 1, device="metal"))
...     for _ in range(3)
... ]
>>> scaler = GradScaler()
>>> for x, y in dataloader:
...     optimizer.zero_grad()
...     with autocast():
...         out = model(x)
...     loss = loss_fn(out.float(), y)
...     scaler.scale(loss).backward()
...     scaler.step(optimizer)
...     scaler.update()
Clipping the unscaled gradients — step sees that
unscale_ already ran and leaves them alone:
>>> from lucid.nn.utils import clip_grad_norm_
>>> x, y = dataloader[0]
>>> optimizer.zero_grad()
>>> scaler.scale(loss_fn(model(x), y)).backward()
>>> scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
>>> norm = clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
>>> scaler.step(optimizer)
>>> scaler.update()
notes:
The canonical training-loop pattern is *scale-loss, then step,
then update*:

1. `scale` multiplies the loss by $s$ before
   `backward()` so the gradients land safely inside fp16 range.
2. `step` unscales the gradients, checks for `inf` /
   `NaN`, and either runs `optimizer.step()` or skips the
   update.
3. `update` adjusts $s$ according to the
   growth / backoff schedule for the next iteration.

To work on the real gradients between `backward()` and the step —
gradient clipping is the usual reason — call `unscale_` first.
The scaler remembers, per optimizer, that its gradients are already
unscaled, so the following `step` does not divide them a second
time.  Each optimizer moves through *ready → unscaled → stepped* once
per iteration and `update` returns every optimizer to *ready*;
calling `unscale_` twice, `unscale_` after `step`, or
`step` twice before `update` raises `RuntimeError`.

With several optimizers on one scaler, an overflow in one optimizer's
gradients skips only that optimizer's step; `update` backs the
scale off if any optimizer overflowed.

The parameters themselves stay float32: `lucid.amp.autocast`
moves the forward pass into half precision, not the weights, so the
gradients arrive in float32 too.  bfloat16 and float64 gradients are
unscaled as well, and unscaling never changes a gradient's dtype.  A
float16 gradient — from a float16 parameter — makes `unscale_`
and `step` raise `ValueError`.

summary: Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) utilities for Lucid.
extended:
Mixed precision training keeps the master copy of parameters and the
loss in float32 while running the bulk of forward / backward compute in
a lower-precision format (float16 or bfloat16). On Apple Silicon this
typically yields a wall-clock speed-up of roughly two times on
compute-bound layers and roughly halves the activation memory
footprint, enabling larger batch sizes or longer context windows.

This subpackage exposes two cooperating tools:

- `autocast` — a context manager that casts eligible ops to a
  lower-precision dtype while leaving reductions and accumulators in
  float32 for numerical safety.
- `GradScaler` — a dynamic loss-scaling helper that prevents
  gradient underflow when training in float16. Tracks an exponential
  scale factor, halving it on detected `inf` / `nan` and growing
  it back up on successful steps.

and the pieces around them:

- `custom_fwd` / `custom_bwd` — decorators that make a custom
  `lucid.autograd.Function` follow the autocast state its `forward`
  ran in, so its `backward` does not meet half-precision gradients with
  float32 saved tensors.
- `is_autocast_available` — whether a device type supports autocast.
examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> import lucid.nn as nn
>>> import lucid.optim as optim
>>> from lucid.amp import autocast, GradScaler
>>> model = nn.Linear(4, 2).to("metal")
>>> optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
>>> x = lucid.randn(8, 4, device="metal")
>>> scaler = GradScaler()
>>> with autocast(device_type="metal", dtype=lucid.float16):
...     out = model(x)  # forward pass, in float16
>>> out.dtype
lucid.float16
>>> loss = out.float().pow(2).mean()
>>> scaler.scale(loss).backward()
>>> scaler.step(optimizer)
>>> scaler.update()
